video.title: Everyone Ignores This Boring Business, But It Makes Him $10M/Year

summary: David Heacock (founder of Filterbuy, a DTC air filter maker) interviews Jake, the 31-year-old president of a second/third-generation family business in Boyertown, Pennsylvania that converts parent rolls into toilet paper, paper towels and dry wipes. Jake's company has about 135 employees, 600 distribution partners in 15 countries and mid-eight-figure revenue, selling bulk truckloads to food-service, janitorial and industrial distributors. David coaches him on growth: model how operations, cash flow, receivables and inventory change before investing in sales, map every target distributor by industry segment and track touch points, and consider selling direct to end users within 200 miles using same-day delivery partners like Roadie. David contrasts this with Filterbuy's vertically integrated model (make for $2, sell for $13, 70% repeat customers). They close on family business advice: split responsibilities cleanly and surface expectations with tools like the 'same page exercise'.

speakers.name: Jake
speakers.description: President of a family tissue/wipes converting business, 31

ideas.name: Tissue and wipes converter selling through distributors
ideas.one_liner: Family business that buys parent rolls from global mills and converts them into toilet paper, paper towels and dry wipes, sold in bulk to food-service, janitorial and industrial distributors.
ideas.business_model: B2B bulk product sales to distributors (half and full truckloads), plus private label
ideas.customer: Distributors: food service (e.g. Sysco), jan-san, industrial; increasingly regional/national distributors and some end users like hotels
ideas.problem: Distributors need flexible suppliers with broad product lines, private label and competitive pricing versus rigid multi-billion-dollar competitors
ideas.offer: About 300 stock SKUs plus about 150 private-label SKUs; delivered pricing with freight built in

pricing.notes: No fuel surcharge; freight built into price so they keep the upside when freight falls. Largest-ever price increase this year due to freight.

acquisition_channels.details: Account executives call distributors with value prop (flexibility, breadth, private label, price) to replace incumbent suppliers.
Trade shows and industry associations suggested as touch points.
Small local mom-and-pop distributors built the base; account exec with national distributor experience opened bigger accounts.

ideas.delivery: Converted in an owned factory in Boyertown, Pennsylvania with domestic partner converters in New York and Miami filling gaps; sales team of 5-6 AEs, a customer loyalty specialist and a sales assistant on HubSpot.
unit_economics_claims: Orders of $15k-50k per half or full truck
ideas.startup_cost: High: machinery, building and inventory (not stated)

acquisition.how: Relationship-driven B2B selling to distributors. UK: cold email to limited-company distributors is allowed under PECR with opt-out; calls must screen CTPS. Trade shows are in person.

onboarding.how: Account setup, quoting and private-label specs handled by a sales assistant and CRM.

delivery.how: Physical converting of 2,000 lb parent rolls on machines in a factory, plus freight.

billing.how: ERP invoicing (Sage 100); credit terms and collections need people.

support.how: Customer loyalty specialist calls accounts; human relationship work.

uk_applicability.notes: Tissue converting and distribution exists in the UK, but freight-heavy low-margin commodity favours regional density; capital intensive.

risks: Thin margins on a commodity product; freight is a large share of cost
Growth consumes cash via receivables and inventory
Overcapacity in back-office departments during fast growth

tactics.name: Model the business before scaling sales
steps: Ask: if sales doubled tomorrow, which departments break (purchasing, customer service, production)?
Financially model margin, equipment, receivables, inventory and cash position at the higher volume
Decide capital allocation (new building, second shift) before hiring salespeople
Commit to the plan so early missteps do not cause you to back off

quote.text: you need to have a plan for all of that before you get too excited about investing in the sales sales piece
quote.speaker: David Heacock

tactics.name: Master target map with tracked touch points
steps: Pick industry segments (hospitals, janitorial, industrial, food service)
Build a master list of every distributor in each segment
Assign a specialist rep per segment
Track calls, emails, trade show meetings per target per quarter in the CRM
Analyse which segments give the most gross profit and pay on time, then staff up there

quote.text: you need to figure out how you're going to track how many touch points each of those each of those targets have with you
quote.speaker: David Heacock

tactics.name: Delivered pricing without surcharges
steps: Quote all prices delivered to the customer's location
Do not show fuel/freight surcharges on invoices (customers expect them to go away)
Keep the margin when freight falls to offset unpassed material increases

quote.text: You put that on an invoice that there's a freight surcharge, they expect it to go away at some point
quote.speaker: Jake

tactics.name: Regional direct-to-end-user delivery
steps: Target end users (hotels, gyms) within about 200 miles of the factory
Truck product daily to a same-day courier sort centre (e.g. Roadie) outside the city
Get it there by 2pm for same-day van delivery
Hire distributor sales reps who already have the relationships

quote.text: if you get product there by um 2:00 p.m., it gets delivered same day
quote.speaker: David Heacock

tactics.name: Same page exercise for family businesses
steps: Bring in a high-EQ consultant
Each family member answers the same ~10 questions on paper separately (revenue target, exit amount, timing)
Read answers to each other to expose misalignment
Then plan how to engineer the outcome the senior generation wants (buyouts, partners)

quote.text: It's called the same page exercise
quote.speaker: Jake

tactics.name: Touch product as few times as possible
steps: Stack filters off the production line; box only when shipping to the end customer
Use multiple distribution points to reach most customers next day

warnings.warning: Selling a business to buyers who do not understand it can see it run into the ground; knowing your business does not mean you can run someone else's.

quote.text: just because you know how to run your business doesn't mean you know how to run someone else's business
quote.speaker: Jake

warnings.warning: Do not start with manufacturing; it needs capital and the sales process is the harder part.

quote.text: I want to start a manufacturing business. I want to do what you're doing. And my advice is is is not to
quote.speaker: Jake

warnings.warning: In distribution, growth consumes cash as receivables and inventory grow, which can force you to back off.

quote.text: the more you grow, the less cash you're going to have
quote.speaker: David Heacock

warnings.warning: Fast sales growth overloaded back-office departments and caused mistakes.

quote.text: They're over capacity and mistakes are happening cuz they're over capacity
quote.speaker: Jake

warnings.warning: Price increases on a commodity product risk losing business and create heavy admin and negotiation work.
Avoiding tough conversations about expectations in a family business sets everyone up for misery.
Leaving estate planning until later is costlier and more painful, especially before a change of control.

lessons.lesson: Boring, unchanging products (toilet paper, filters) offer stability because demand will exist in 50 years regardless of AI.

quote.text: Doesn't matter what AI model you're on
quote.speaker: David Heacock

lessons.lesson: Choose products customers use up and rebuy so you are not hunting for a new customer each sale.

quote.text: He hated having to go find a new customer every time he sold it
quote.speaker: Jake

lessons.lesson: Revenue alone does not make you more money; business model and quality of revenue do.

quote.text: the revenue doesn't make you more money more money. It's your business model that makes you more money
quote.speaker: David Heacock

lessons.lesson: Middlemen face compressed margins; owning the end-customer relationship compounds.
In freight-heavy low-margin products, business density clusters near the factory.

quote.text: the closer you are to our factory, the more business we have. Cuz freight is such a big component on a small margin item
quote.speaker: Jake

lessons.lesson: Segment customers by profitability and payment behaviour; you could fire 10% of customers and make more money.

quote.text: you could fire 10% of your customers, have less sales, have more money in your pocket
quote.speaker: David Heacock

lessons.lesson: In family businesses, split responsibilities cleanly and define final decision rights.

quote.text: Split your responsibilities very cleanly amongst family members
quote.speaker: Jake

lessons.lesson: Get clarity on the outcome you want, then reverse engineer the business plan; keep refining it like polishing a marble.
Partner with channels that have a genuine advantage (e.g. Walmart pickup) and serve directly where they do not.
Do estate planning early to minimise tax and control problems at succession.

evidence_quality.rationale: Two first-hand operators with specific numbers (Filterbuy figures detailed; Jake's revenue only as a range). Host coaches guest; no product promotion beyond Filterbuy mention.
